new_entities.name: Progressive overload resistance training
new_entities.description: Resistance training that systematically increases load, volume, or other overload variables over time to sustain adaptation.

new_entities.name: Long-term strength gain
new_entities.description: The increase in maximal muscular strength achieved over weeks to months of training.

edges.effect_quant: The current evidence base supports progressive resistance training as one of the most reliable ways to improve strength over time. A 2004 meta-analysis of 621 healthy participants found that multiple-set progression becomes superior to single-set work as training continues, while a 2013 review reported that high-intensity progressive resistance training improved lower-limb strength more than lower intensities in older adults (SMD 0.79, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.17).
edges.population: healthy adults performing resistance training over at least several weeks
edges.mechanism: When training stress is increased progressively, muscles and the nervous system continue receiving a stimulus large enough to drive further adaptation rather than plateauing after the beginner phase.
edges.summary: This is a foundational training edge rather than a trendy intervention, and the evidence is correspondingly strong. If the goal is long-term strength, some form of progressive overload is not optional; it is the basic mechanism that keeps adaptation moving.
edges.caveats: The exact way overload is progressed can vary. More load is not always better every session, and factors such as recovery, exercise selection, and total weekly volume still shape the final result.
